articles.title: Numbers in brand names make consumers expect tastier food
articles.summary: A new study reveals that including numbers in food and beverage brand names makes consumers expect a better, more complex taste. Writing the numbers as words rather than digits amplifies this effect even further.

articles.title: Higher aerobic fitness is linked to lower heart rates during acute stress
articles.summary: A new study reveals that people with higher aerobic capacity experience lower heart rates during acute stress. However, fitness doesn't seem to blunt the body's hormonal or psychological stress responses, regardless of the type of stressor.

articles.title: Psychologists studied adult webcam interactions and found a surprising relationship dynamic
articles.summary: Are online adult webcam relationships purely transactional? A new study suggests otherwise, finding that emotional intimacy and personal investment play a surprisingly large role in keeping both performers and paying viewers committed to their digital connections.

articles.title: Your gut may help your brain decide what to remember
articles.summary: Signals traveling from the gut to the brain may help turn meals into lasting memories. Rats showed stronger memory activity after consuming nutritious foods, but not after drinking sweet liquids with little or no nutritional value. Blocking the vagus nerve erased this effect and made it harder for the animals to remember where food had been located. Over time, diets high in fat and sugar also weakened this memory system.

articles.title: How culture shapes the psychological costs of narcissism
articles.summary: Is narcissism always a recipe for unhappiness? A large international study reveals that while seeking admiration boosts personal well-being globally, the psychological cost of a hostile ego depends heavily on the cultural values of the society you live in.

articles.title: Willpower is linked to eco-friendly habits, but short-term boosts in self-discipline fall short
articles.summary: People with naturally high self-control generally maintain more eco-friendly habits. However, new longitudinal research reveals that short-term bursts of willpower do not instantly improve green routines, suggesting society should focus on designing effortless environmental systems instead.

articles.title: Inside the Backrooms: The internet’s creepiest place is becoming a tourist attraction
articles.summary: The Backrooms began as a single eerie image of empty yellow rooms, but internet users transformed it into a vast fictional world that feels disturbingly real. Through videos, games, maps, survival guides and social media stories, audiences do more than watch the horror unfold. They help build and explore it. Researchers suggest this popularity reflects a new kind of digital tourism, where people emotionally enter imaginary places filled with mystery, nostalgia and unease.

articles.summary: A genetic analysis provides evidence that a higher body weight might directly cause thinning in specific brain areas. This structural change tends to overlap with high levels of inflammation and internal fat.

articles.title: Overactive immune cells might drive nerve pain in long COVID
articles.summary: Millions of people with long COVID suffer from persistent nerve pain and fatigue. A new review of existing literature suggests that overactive immune cells known as mast cells might be directly responsible for damaging the body's fragile nerve fibers.

articles.title: Eating within 8 hours may help keep the aging brain sharp
articles.summary: Eating within a shorter daily window may help protect certain thinking skills as people age. In a small six-month trial, older women who limited eating to about 8 to 9 hours a day performed better on planning and problem-solving tests than those who ate over 12 hours. Both groups lost similar amounts of weight, hinting that when people eat could matter in addition to how much they eat.

articles.title: A hidden Alzheimer’s tipping point may decide who gets dementia
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a possible tipping point that helps determine whether Alzheimer’s-related brain changes lead to dementia. The key may lie in how the brain’s immune cells respond to plaques and tau, offering a promising new target for treatments designed to extend cognitive resilience.
